difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY - one concept (a fully-connected layer has one weight per pair of neurons in consecutive layers) and a single short computation over three layer pairs, well under 1.5 minutes.
stem:
Consider a fully-connected feed-forward multi-layer perceptron. It has 30 neurons in the input layer, followed by two hidden layers and an output layer. The first hidden layer has 4 neurons and the second hidden layer has 3 neurons. The output layer has only one neuron. Assume that no bias parameters are used.

The number of learnable parameters in the multi-layer perceptron is __________ . (Answer in **integer**)

solution.quick: With no biases, the only learnable parameters of a fully-connected network are its weights, one for every connection between consecutive layers. The layer sizes $30 \to 4 \to 3 \to 1$ give $30 \times 4 + 4 \times 3 + 3 \times 1 = 120 + 12 + 3 =$ **135**.

steps.title: What counts as a learnable parameter
steps.body:
In a fully-connected feed-forward MLP, every neuron in layer $l-1$ feeds every neuron in layer $l$, and each such connection carries one trainable weight. Between a layer of $n_{l-1}$ neurons and a layer of $n_l$ neurons there is a weight matrix

$$
W^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l \times n_{l-1}}, \qquad \text{with } n_{l-1}\, n_l \text{ entries}.
$$

A bias vector would add $n_l$ more parameters per layer, but the question says **no bias parameters** are used. The 30 input "neurons" only hold the input features; they have no parameters of their own.

steps.title: List the layer sizes
steps.body:
Input → first hidden → second hidden → output:

$$
30 \;\to\; 4 \;\to\; 3 \;\to\; 1 ,
$$

so there are three weight matrices, one for each pair of consecutive layers.

steps.title: Count the weights in each block
steps.body:
| Connection | Shape of $W$ | Weights |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input (30) → Hidden 1 (4) | $4 \times 30$ | $30 \times 4 = 120$ |
| Hidden 1 (4) → Hidden 2 (3) | $3 \times 4$ | $4 \times 3 = 12$ |
| Hidden 2 (3) → Output (1) | $1 \times 3$ | $3 \times 1 = 3$ |

steps.title: Add them up
steps.body:
$$
120 + 12 + 3 = 135 .
$$

Answer: **135**. For comparison, a bias on every hidden and output neuron would add $4 + 3 + 1 = 8$ parameters, giving $143$, but the question excludes biases.

solution.teaching:
**Anatomy of a multi-layer perceptron.** An MLP is a stack of layers. The input layer simply presents the feature vector $x$; it computes nothing and stores no parameters. Each later layer $l$ (hidden or output) computes

$$
h^{(l)} = \sigma\!\left(W^{(l)} h^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)}\right),
$$

where $h^{(l-1)}$ is the previous layer's output, $W^{(l)}$ is the weight matrix, $b^{(l)}$ is the bias vector and $\sigma$ is an activation function such as ReLU or sigmoid. Standard activations have no trainable parameters.

**Counting parameters.** "Fully connected" means every neuron of layer $l-1$ is wired to every neuron of layer $l$, so $W^{(l)}$ has $n_l$ rows and $n_{l-1}$ columns, which is $n_{l-1} n_l$ weights. The bias adds $n_l$ more. For layer sizes $n_0, n_1, \dots, n_L$:

$$
\#\text{params} = \sum_{l=1}^{L} \big(n_{l-1} n_l + n_l\big) \quad\text{(with biases)}, \qquad \sum_{l=1}^{L} n_{l-1} n_l \quad\text{(without biases)}.
$$

A useful picture: draw the network as a layered graph; the weights are the **edges** and the biases sit on the non-input **nodes**. Counting parameters is counting edges (plus non-input nodes if biases are used).

**Why it matters.** The parameter count measures model capacity and memory cost. Notice here that the first layer dominates: $120$ of the $135$ weights connect the $30$ inputs to the first hidden layer. Wide inputs make the first layer expensive.

**Connecting to this question.** The layers are $30 \to 4 \to 3 \to 1$ with no biases, so we count only edges: $30 \cdot 4 + 4 \cdot 3 + 3 \cdot 1 = 120 + 12 + 3 = 135$.
solution.shortcut: No biases ⇒ add the products of consecutive layer sizes: $30\cdot4 + 4\cdot3 + 3\cdot1 = 135$. If biases are used, add the number of non-input neurons ($4 + 3 + 1$).
solution.commonTrap: Adding biases out of habit ($135 + 8 = 143$) even though the question says no bias parameters are used, or treating the input layer as if it had parameters. Another slip is multiplying all layer sizes together ($30 \times 4 \times 3 \times 1 = 360$) instead of summing the products of **consecutive** layers.

answerVerification.method: Blind independent re-solve + Python check agrees with official key
answerVerification.checkCode:
layers = [30, 4, 3, 1]              # input, hidden1, hidden2, output
weights = [a * b for a, b in zip(layers, layers[1:])]   # 120, 12, 3
total = sum(weights)                # no biases
with_bias = sum(a * b + b for a, b in zip(layers, layers[1:]))
print(weights, total, 'with biases would be', with_bias)
assert total == 135
answerVerification.notes: Independent verifier solved from show-question output and the official crop before reading the key or the stored solution. With no biases the only parameters are the weights between consecutive fully-connected layers 30 -> 4 -> 3 -> 1: 30*4 = 120, 4*3 = 12, 3*1 = 3, total 135 (Python confirms; with biases it would be 143). Independent answer 135 matches the official key 135 to 135 (NAT, 2 marks).
